# 2025 Enderlin Tornado

The 2025 Enderlin tornado was a violent and exceptionally rare atmospheric phenomenon that struck southeastern North Dakota on June 20, 2025 , . Officially classified as an EF-5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, it marked a significant event in American meteorological history due to its intensity and its status as the first such tornado confirmed in the United States since the 2013 Moore, Oklahoma tornado , , . The storm originated from a powerful mesoscale convective system that also produced widespread straight-line winds through a derecho, impacting a broad swath of northern states and southern Canada between June 19 and June 22, 2025 . The tornado carved a destructive path approximately 12 miles long and over a mile wide, causing catastrophic damage to farmsteads and infrastructure along its trajectory , . Its confirmation as an EF-5 following extensive forensic analysis by the National Weather Service (NWS) Grand Forks office highlighted the extreme forces at play, with evidence including the derailing and displacement of dozens of railroad cars weighing hundreds of thousands of pounds , . The event claimed the lives of three individuals in rural areas east of the town of Enderlin, while the city itself sustained only power-related disruptions , . The tornado's occurrence in North Dakota represents a historical anomaly, being the first EF-5 to be confirmed in the state since the devastating 1957 Fargo tornado, which occurred exactly 68 years earlier .

## Meteorological History and Official Rating

The 2025 Enderlin tornado was the product of a highly unstable weather regime that developed across the northern Great Plains . It formed within a larger, powerful severe thunderstorm complex that evolved into a radar-defined derecho—a widespread, long-lived wind storm associated with a band of rapidly moving showers or thunderstorms—which affected central and eastern North Dakota, as well as adjacent parts of Minnesota . The tornado specifically touched down just before midnight local time on June 20, 2025 . Different official records provide slightly varying but consistent timestamps for this critical moment. One source indicates the tornado began its ground contact at 11:02 p.m. Central Daylight Time (CDT), which corresponds to 04:02 UTC . Another official database entry places the time of the event near Enderlin Airport at 22:04 CST (04:04 UTC) , . Regardless of the exact minute, the event occurred late in the evening, catching many residents off guard. The tornado's duration was remarkably brief but intensely destructive, lasting for approximately 19 minutes before it lifted off the ground . It dissipated around 11:21 p.m. CDT (04:21 UTC) .

Initially, the National Weather Service (NWS) conducted a preliminary assessment of the damage and assigned the tornado an Enhanced Fujita (EF) rating of at least EF-3 , . This initial rating reflected the significant destruction observed, particularly the leveling of homes and farmsteads. However, subsequent, more detailed post-storm forensic analysis, conducted by NWS meteorologists in Grand Forks in collaboration with engineers and wind damage experts, revealed far greater levels of destruction than initially apparent , . This extended investigation led to the official upgrade of the tornado's rating to EF-5, the highest possible classification on the scale, signifying catastrophic damage resulting from unimaginable wind forces , . The official confirmation of this upgraded rating occurred on or before December 17, 2025, with one report specifying the date of the upgrade announcement as October 6, 2025 , , . The decision to elevate the rating was not arbitrary; it was based on a rigorous examination of specific, high-end damage indicators that could only be explained by winds exceeding 200 mph .

The primary evidence supporting the EF-5 classification came from the analysis of damage to industrial and transportation infrastructure. A key indicator was the derailment of 33 train cars on CPKC's Elbow Lake Subdivision southeast of Enderlin , . The force required to dislodge and hurl these massive railcars is a benchmark for assessing the most intense tornadoes. Specifically, the analysis noted that fully loaded grain hopper cars, weighing up to 286,000 pounds, were tipped over completely . Even more dramatically, empty railroad tanker cars, some weighing as much as 72,000 pounds, were lofted and thrown considerable distances . One such empty tanker car was found tossed 475.5 feet (approximately 144.9 meters) south of County Road 46 , . These specific, quantifiable examples of vehicle displacement provided concrete physical proof of the wind speeds. Other corroborating damage indicators included the complete destruction of farmsteads, which were swept clean to their bare foundations or even basement levels, the debarking of trees, the bending of steel electrical transmission towers, and the uprooting of large tree root balls near the Maple River , , . The combination of these extreme damage signatures allowed forecasters to confidently assign the EF-5 rating, confirming it as the first such tornado in the United States since the 2013 Moore, Oklahoma event and the 11th overall since the Enhanced Fujita scale was adopted in 2007 , .

## Path of Destruction and Damage Analysis

The Enderlin tornado's path of destruction was both long and exceptionally wide, carving a scar across the landscape of southeastern North Dakota , . Officially documented in the NOAA Storm Events Database, the tornado's track began approximately three miles east of the town of Enderlin, near the border of Cass and Ransom Counties, and was geolocated specifically to the area of "ENDERLIN ARPT" (Airport) in RANSOM CO. , . The tornado moved generally northeastward, traversing a distance of 12.1 miles (19.47 km) before lifting . At its widest point, the funnel cloud spanned 1.05 miles (1.69 km or 1.7 km), creating a vast zone of devastation , , . The intensity of the tornado varied along its path, transitioning from a lower-rated EF-2 strength when it first impacted the ADM Edible Bean Specialties facility at 136th Avenue SE and County Road 136, to its full EF-5 fury as it crossed the CPKC railway line southeast of Enderlin .

The damage inflicted by the EF-5 winds was catastrophic and indiscriminate. The most compelling evidence of its power came from the obliteration of industrial-scale assets. As previously noted, the derailment of 33 train cars was a primary factor in the rating upgrade . The force of the wind was sufficient to completely topple fully loaded grain hopper cars, some of which weighed as much as 286,000 pounds, and to throw empty, 72,000-pound railroad tanker cars great distances . This level of structural disruption is indicative of winds that can exceed 200 mph. Beyond the railways, the tornado systematically destroyed every structure in its direct path. Farmsteads were completely leveled, leaving behind only bare foundations or the concrete slabs of basements, a classic signature of EF-5 intensity , . Two homes were entirely destroyed, killing two people inside one residence . A third person was killed when the tornado passed directly over another home northwest of the highway . The sheer power of the vortex stripped trees of their bark, snapped them like twigs, and uprooted entire trees, sometimes displacing their massive root balls , . Steel electrical transmission towers, designed to withstand significant stress, were visibly bent and twisted by the wind, further testifying to the storm's ferocity , .

In stark contrast to the devastation along its main path, the city of Enderlin itself experienced a relatively minor impact. While the surrounding rural areas were subjected to EF-5 winds, the urban core of Enderlin sustained primarily power-related issues, with approximately 24,000 customers losing electricity across the state due to the broader storm system , . The tornado's immense energy was focused in a narrow corridor east of the town, sparing the populated center. However, the psychological impact on the community was undoubtedly profound, given the proximity of such a catastrophic event. The storm also caused significant collateral damage, including the blowing over of a cell tower, which would have disrupted communication services in the area . The overall damage profile, characterized by the complete removal of buildings from their foundations and the violent displacement of heavy objects, left no doubt in the minds of the forensic survey teams that they were dealing with a truly exceptional and deadly storm.

## Human Toll and Casualty Reports

The human cost of the 2025 Enderlin tornado was tragically clear, with three lives lost in the rural communities east of the town of Enderlin , . Local law enforcement and emergency responders worked diligently to account for all residents in the heavily damaged area. The Cass County Sheriff’s Office played a crucial role in confirming the fatalities. During a press conference held on June 22, 2025, Sheriff Jesse Jahner announced the grim discovery of two individuals who had been found deceased at a residence located east of Highway 46 near 140th Avenue SE . He later specified that a third fatality was discovered at a second, nearby residence north of the first location . Following a comprehensive grid search of the entire damage area, officials confirmed that no additional fatalities or major injuries were found .

The identities of the victims were released by the Cass County Sheriff’s Office on June 22, 2025 . The three individuals who lost their lives were:
* Michael Dalton Dehn, 73 years old.
* Katherine Ann Pfaff-Dehn, 73 years old.
* Marcario Machuca Lucio, 89 years old.
All three were residents of Enderlin, North Dakota . Their deaths underscore the peril faced by those caught outside in mobile homes or poorly constructed buildings during such a powerful tornado. The news of the fatalities was widely reported by local media outlets, including KVRR Local News, which covered the aftermath and the recovery efforts . Some reports indicated that storm chasers may have been among the first to locate the bodies of two of the victims, highlighting the chaotic and tragic nature of the scene immediately following the tornado's passage . One storm chaser, John Farley, described the experience of finding the deceased as "the worst chase ever," emphasizing the somber reality of witnessing the human toll of these events firsthand .

A significant point of discrepancy exists regarding the official death toll. While multiple credible news sources and statements from the Cass County Sheriff’s Office confirm three fatalities, the NOAA Storm Events Database, which serves as the authoritative national repository for verified storm data, lists the number of direct and indirect deaths as zero , . This conflict requires careful consideration. The news reports and official statements from local law enforcement likely reflect immediate investigations and public announcements made shortly after the disaster. In contrast, the NOAA database entry, last updated on December 17, 2025, represents the consolidated, officially vetted data from the National Weather Service's storm survey . The reason for this discrepancy is not detailed in the provided sources, but it could stem from various factors, such as the official NWS survey classifying the deaths as indirect rather than direct tornado causes, or potentially a lack of definitive attribution in the formal data entry process. For the purposes of this report, the more detailed and corroborated accounts from law enforcement and media—confirming three fatalities—are presented as the factual narrative, while the conflicting data from the NOAA database is noted as an official record. No injuries were officially reported as a direct result of the tornado .

## Regional Context and Broader Weather System

The 2025 Enderlin tornado was not an isolated event but rather the most violent manifestation of a large and prolonged severe weather episode that gripped the northern plains from June 19 through June 22, 2025 . This multi-day period saw a succession of powerful storms affecting a vast area that included northern U.S. states like Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota, and South Dakota, as well as southern Canada, particularly Saskatchewan . The overarching system responsible for the Enderlin tornado was a potent derecho, a widespread, long-lived wind storm associated with a band of strong thunderstorms . This derecho complex produced widespread straight-line wind damage, with hurricane-force winds reaching up to 120 mph recorded across several states . The Enderlin tornado was embedded within this larger system, meaning it formed from a supercell thunderstorm that was part of the broader mesoscale convective system that defined the derecho .

The severity of the storm system was evident in the sheer number of severe weather events it spawned. Across North Dakota alone, the NOAA Storm Events Database recorded a total of 39 separate severe weather events between June 20 and June 21, 2025 . This included 15 distinct tornadoes, ranging from EF0 to the violent EF5, as well as 22 thunderstorm wind events, one hail event, and one flash flood . The Enderlin EF-5 was one of several violent tornadoes to strike the region during this outbreak. Other significant tornadoes included an EF-4 that touched down in Elizabeth, Cass County, and an EF-3 in Urbana . This concentration of intense tornado activity underscores the extreme instability and wind shear present in the atmosphere during this period. The presence of multiple violent tornadoes within a single storm complex is a testament to the exceptional meteorological conditions that prevailed.

Beyond the direct threat of tornadoes, the derecho component of the storm system caused widespread and significant secondary impacts. The most notable of these was a catastrophic blow to the region's agricultural sector. According to ND Agriculture Commissioner Doug Goehring, the prolonged, damaging winds associated with the derecho complex resulted in an estimated loss of 50 to 80 million bushels of grain storage capacity . This figure highlights the immense economic toll the storm took on the farming industry, which is a cornerstone of the North Dakota economy. Additionally, the storm system triggered widespread power outages, affecting approximately 24,000 customers in North Dakota . These cascading effects—from the violent tornadoes to the widespread wind damage and agricultural losses—paint a picture of a truly multi-faceted regional disaster that tested the resilience of communities and infrastructure across a large geographic area.

## Aftermath, Legacy, and Official Documentation

The aftermath of the 2025 Enderlin tornado was characterized by a massive recovery effort focused on clearing debris, restoring power, and providing support to affected families . While details on specific government aid programs or long-term rebuilding initiatives are not available in the provided sources, the immediate response involved local emergency services, state resources, and likely federal assistance through agencies like FEMA. The destruction was concentrated in rural areas, requiring specialized equipment and personnel to navigate the devastated landscapes and assist survivors. The psychological impact on the community of Enderlin and the surrounding counties was profound, as residents grappled with the loss of life, property, and the traumatic memory of the event .

The legacy of the Enderlin tornado is firmly rooted in its rarity and historical significance. For meteorologists and climatologists, its confirmation as an EF-5 is a landmark event. It ended a long drought of such violent tornadoes in the United States, marking the first EF-5 to be officially recorded since the devastating May 20, 2013, tornado that struck Moore, Oklahoma , , . This 12-year gap without a U.S. EF-5 tornado made the Enderlin event a subject of intense scientific interest and discussion. Furthermore, its occurrence in North Dakota was historically unprecedented. The tornado was the first EF-5 to be confirmed in the state since the infamous April 9, 1957, tornado that ravaged the Fargo-Moorhead area, an event that occurred exactly 68 years prior to the Enderlin tornado , . This historical parallel underscores the extraordinary nature of the event and its place in the annals of North Dakota's weather history.

The official documentation of the event is maintained by several authoritative bodies, ensuring a standardized record for future reference. The primary source for verified meteorological data is the NOAA Storm Events Database, which compiles information from official NWS storm surveys . This database contains the official statistics for the Enderlin tornado, including its path length, width, timing, and final EF-5 rating , . As noted, however, this official record contains discrepancies, such as the reported zero fatalities, which differ from accounts from local law enforcement and news media , . Despite these inconsistencies, the database remains the definitive source for the storm's physical parameters. The detailed forensic analysis conducted by the NWS Grand Forks office, which led to the EF-5 upgrade, will serve as a case study for future storm surveys, providing a rich dataset of damage indicators used to classify extreme tornado intensity , . In summary, the 2025 Enderlin tornado stands as a powerful reminder of nature's destructive potential and a significant chapter in the ongoing study of severe weather in the United States.

Enderlin tornado upgraded to EF-5 after extensive review
========================================================

##### Estimated peak winds at least 210 mph

![Image 1: Enderlin, ND, tornado on June 20, 2025](https://gray-kvly-prod.gtv-cdn.com/resizer/v2/7AKTZZCR7VA5BLURUPAFOPNIY4.jpeg?auth=c315c35716123cf24e0c0e5b2e8d63708c9bb2919a9ca0ba720f57d98e0d471a&width=800&height=450&smart=true)

Enderlin, ND, tornado on June 20, 2025(Darren Stave / SkySpy Photos)

By [Summer Schnellbach](https://www.valleynewslive.com/authors/Summer%20Schnellbach/)

Published: Oct. 6, 2025 at 10:49 AM CDT

FARGO, N.D. (Valley News Live) -

The Enderlin, ND tornado from June 20, 2025 that claimed three lives has officially been upgraded to an EF-5 from the National Weather Service of Grand Forks. This comes after further extensive review including forensic damage wind speed estimates.

The original preliminary rating of the tornado was an EF-3 with estimated peak winds of 160 mph, but that was subject to further review. Upon further review with the help of forensic wind analysis, the estimated peak winds were at least 210 mph. Evidence examined included several fully-loaded grain hopper cars that were toppled over, and the lofting of tanker cars, including one empty tanker car that was tossed about 475.5 feet, according to the National Weather Service.

Meteorologists use specific damage indicators such as buildings/structures, trees, towers, etc. to assess the estimated wind speed of a tornado. This was a unique case because derailed and lofted train cars is not a defined damage indicator. The NWS partnered with engineers and scientists from the Northern Tornado Project at Western University to determine what the wind speeds would have needed to be to topple the fully-loaded train cars.

Damage to trees near the Maple River east of Enderlin was also reanalyzed and found that root balls were displaced. The NWS says that the new peak wind estimate also more closely correlates to the storm-relative velocity data from the radar. The tornado had a path just over 12 miles long and had a maximum width of just over 1 mile.

This is the first EF-5 tornado in the US since Moore, Oklahoma in 2013, and the first EF-5 in ND since the Fargo Tornado of 1957.

Tornado outbreak and derecho of June 19–22, 2025

Radar loop of the derecho as it passed over North Dakota, Minnesota and other states and Ontario, Canada on June 20 through the night of June 21.

Meteorological history
DurationJune 19–22, 2025
Tornado outbreak
Tornadoes40
Maximum ratingEF5 tornado
Highest windsTornadic – >210 mph (340 km/h) (Enderlin, North Dakota EF5 on June 20)
Largest hail4 in (10 cm) near the Jamestown Dam on June 20th[1]
Derecho
Highest gusts120 mph (190 km/h) (Beltrami County, Minnesota)[2]
Maximum rainfall6.5 in (170 mm) (Chenango County, New York)[3]
Overall effects
Fatalities7 (6 tornadic, 1 from downburst)
Injuries>4
Damage$875 million (2025 USD)
Areas affectedNorthern United States (Great Plains), Southern Canada, Northeastern United States
Part of the tornado outbreaks of 2025
A significant [tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak") and associated powerful [derecho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derecho "Derecho") caused major damage across the northern [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and parts of southern [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada") on June 19–22, 2025. At least one other tornado was confirmed in [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota") the same day.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4) The following day, the National Weather Service in Grand Forks confirmed that [a powerful tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Enderlin_tornado "2025 Enderlin tornado"), later rated EF5 a few months after, killed three people east of [Enderlin, North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enderlin,_North_Dakota "Enderlin, North Dakota").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-5) The derecho also produced hurricane-force winds across Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota, and South Dakota, with the highest confirmed wind gust reaching 120 mph (190 km/h). Many tornadoes touched down in the Canadian province of [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan "Saskatchewan") as well. The same system produced another squall line that produced damaging wind, several downburst, and flash flooding in southern [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") on June 21 with one person being killed by a downburst.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CPnug-7) This line of storms would push into northern [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_/(state/) "New York (state)") early on June 22 and spawn a deadly EF1 tornado that killed three people in [Clark Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Mills,_New_York "Clark Mills, New York").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMsurvey-8) It also caused widespread wind damage and flash flooding.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMcleanup-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmnyt-10) In all, the storm system caused seven fatalities and produced 40 tornadoes, causing $875 million in damages.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-11) The outbreak saw the first EF5-rated tornado in over 12 years. Meteorological synopsis ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Meteorological synopsis")\] The [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) had been monitoring favorable conditions for storm development in the Northern Plains/Upper Midwest region since June 18, noting limited low-level moisture and instability with modest wind shear yet steep [lapse rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lapse_rate "Lapse rate") allowing for the development of weak thunderstorms in the area, which could in turn create a threat for isolated wind gusts and large hail.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-12) Although an upper-level [ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ridge_/(meteorology/) "Ridge (meteorology)") was present throughout this region on June 19, a weak mid-level [shortwave trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortwave_/(meteorology/) "Shortwave (meteorology)") moved over the [Canadian Prairies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Prairies "Canadian Prairies") which, in combination with a strengthening low-level jet and the advection of warm, moist air, allowed for robust thunderstorm development with the primary threat being large hail and isolated strong wind gusts.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-13) [![Image 3: The National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center outlined a moderate risk (oval colored in red) area for severe weather over portions of North Dakota and Minnesota on this map.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/SPC_20250621_0100Z_Day_1_outlook.gif/250px-SPC_20250621_0100Z_Day_1_outlook.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPC_20250621_0100Z_Day_1_outlook.gif) [![Image 4: This version of the map shows a 10% probability of a tornado within 25 miles of a given point in the highest risk area, and a 10% chance of a significant tornado.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/SPC_20250621_0100Z_Day_1_tornado_outlook.gif/250px-SPC_20250621_0100Z_Day_1_tornado_outlook.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPC_20250621_0100Z_Day_1_tornado_outlook.gif) SPC outlooks issued at 01Z, about three hours before the tornado touched down. A [wind-driven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derecho "Derecho") moderate risk was issued for the area, although the possibility of a strong tornado was mentioned.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-14) On June 15, the [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) noted on its Day 6 outlook that a shortwave, mid-level ridge was forecasted to traverse into the upper [Mississippi River valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River "Mississippi River") and remain over the region as mid-level heights increase. Beneath the ridge, a moist and unstable airmass was expected to be in place from the lower to mid-Missouri Valley, northeastward into the western [Great Lakes region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_region "Great Lakes region"). Instability and deep-layer shear were sufficient for a localized severe threat, though uncertainties remained on where the greatest potential for convection would be.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:5-15) A seasonally strong mid-level trough was forecast to eject over the Northern Plains on June 20, which featured moderate upper-level divergence to promote lift and shear support.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:5-15) The [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) Day 2 outlook mentioned that "a small area of uncapped and very unstable air mass, perhaps over northeast SD and southeast ND. Here, a conditional supercell and tornado risk will exist ... very large hail and tornadoes appear likely."[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-16) [![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/0156_Spiritwood%2C_ND_EF3.png/330px-0156_Spiritwood%2C_ND_EF3.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:0156_Spiritwood,_ND_EF3.png) A radar scan of a supercell producing a large EF3 tornado near Spiritwood, North Dakota. Supercells began developing across eastern North Dakota, around the [Jamestown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamestown,_North_Dakota "Jamestown, North Dakota") area, in the evening hours of June 20. Although they were initially elevated, the strengthening low-level jet and isentropic/geostrophic ascent contributed to eroding the convective inhibition that was in place, allowing them to become more surface-based.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:3-17) Additionally, a nearby frontal boundary provided extreme [storm-relative helicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm-relative_helicity "Storm-relative helicity") which further supported surface-based shear and streamwise vorticity as well as development of rotation or mesocyclogenesis within the supercells.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:3-17) Confirmed tornadoes ------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025&action=edit§ion=4 "Edit section: Confirmed tornadoes")\]

After crossing a ridge near the Sheyenne River, the tornado caused widespread tree damage and struck up to four more homes south of Valley City. One home suffered the most severe damage, with collapsed exterior top-floor walls, total roof destruction, and the complete collapse of a garage. A nearby carport and shed were also partially collapsed. Another home had roof and siding damage with one exterior wall pushed inward. Additional nearby homes experienced window, siding, and shingle damage. Tree damage continued in the area with numerous fallen branches before the tornado lifted.[28]

Nearby, power lines were brought down and part of a large shop building housing equipment was torn away before the tornado lifted.[36]

This large, violent, and deadly tornado touched down at 11:02 p.m. CDT south of Enderlin, initially snapping tree branches at EF0 intensity. The tornado intensified and widened as it moved northeastward across County Road 55 through open fields. The tornado then impacted the ADM Edible Bean Specialties facility at the corner of 136th Avenue SE and County Road 136 at EF2 strength, snapping large trees and destroying an outbuilding.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT2-49) The tornado then rapidly intensified as it continued northeastward, reaching EF5 intensity as it crossed [CPKC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Pacific_Kansas_City "Canadian Pacific Kansas City")'s [Elbow Lake Subdivision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbow_Lake_Subdivision "Elbow Lake Subdivision") southeast of Enderlin, derailing several train cars on a stopped freight train, including one empty tanker car that was thrown 475.5 feet (144.9 m) south of [ND 46](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_Highway_46 "North Dakota Highway 46").[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:22-50) Initially, this damage was left unrated, but further analysis determined that there was forensic damage of the lofting of empty tanker cars weighing up to 72,000 pounds (33,000 kg) and tipping over fully loaded grain hopper cars weighing up to 286,000 pounds (130,000 kg) each. Based on this, the rating for this location was upgraded to EF5 with wind speeds greater than 210 mph (340 km/h) on October 6, 2025, the first F5/EF5 tornado to occur in North Dakota since the [Fargo tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo_tornado "Fargo tornado") exactly 68 years prior.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:22-50) Continuing north, the tornado blew over a cell tower, damaged crop fields, and snapped large trees, debarking some of them. A farmhouse was also swept away, and nearby outbuildings were destroyed. Crossing the highway, two houses were particularly devastated, with two fatalities occurring in the area. The first was swept away while the other was leveled.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-:1-51) The tornado then began to turn northwest, leveling another home, which caused another fatality, and bending over tall steel electrical transmission towers before weakening and dissipating at 11:21 p.m. CDT.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4) Overall, the tornado was on the ground for 19 minutes, had a path length of 12.10 miles (19.47 km), and reached a peak width of 1.05 miles (1.69 km). The tornado was the first to be rated EF5 on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale") since the [Moore, Oklahoma, tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Moore_tornado "2013 Moore tornado") on May 20, 2013,[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-52) and was the first F5/EF5 tornado to occur in North Dakota since the [Fargo tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fargo_tornado "Fargo tornado") exactly 68 years prior.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-53) ### Clark Mills–Clinton, New York \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Clark Mills–Clinton, New York")\]

The same line of thunderstorms associated with the earlier derecho continued to move across the [Northern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_United_States "Northern United States") and Southern [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), reaching [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_/(state/) "New York (state)") by the early morning of June 22.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmfox-54) This deadly QLCS tornado formed along a kink in this line, affecting the hamlet of [Clark Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Mills,_New_York "Clark Mills, New York"), where three people were killed. The tornado first touched down within Clark Mills and moved southwestward through the hamlet, where it snapped or uprooted many trees.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMsurvey-8) In this area, three people were killed when downed trees cut through and crushed their houses. In one house, six-year-old twin girls were killed by a tree that sliced through it, and a 50-year-old woman was killed in another location when a tree fell through the roof and crushed one end of her home; all victims were pronounced dead on the scene.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cmnyt-10)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMcleanup-9) Overall, this made the tornado the second-deadliest in New York state history.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-55) The tornado then turned sharply to the south, destroying a historic [grist mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grist_mill "Grist mill") near [Oriskany Creek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriskany_Creek "Oriskany Creek") with nearby heavy machinery being tossed into the creek. Continuing south, it began to move through more rural areas, causing more tree damage before turning southeast and dissipating.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-DAT-4)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CMsurvey-8) While a [tornado warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_warning "Tornado warning") was issued for south-central [Oneida County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneida_County,_New_York "Oneida County, New York") due to radar-indicated rotation,[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-56) the tornado initially formed outside of the polygon in an area that was just under a severe thunderstorm warning, although it did have a tornado possible tag. This was due to the warning being for another EF1 tornado that formed around the same time to the west of this one. Additionally, the rotation was assessed as being much farther south than it actually was.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-57) This meant that not all of Clark Mills’ residents, including the three victims and their families, received the warning; many residents confirmed that they did not receive any warning. The early-morning time of this tornado also meant that most people were asleep as it touched down, so the warning may not have been able to reach them. It was further clarified that the [recent staffing cuts to NOAA and the NWS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOAA_in_the_second_Trump_administration "NOAA in the second Trump administration") did not affect the [Binghamton office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service_Binghamton,_New_York "National Weather Service Binghamton, New Severe thunderstorms moved into southern [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") on the evening of June 21 and the early morning of June 22, causing widespread wind damage and several [downbursts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downburst "Downburst"). The [Samuel de Champlain Provincial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_de_Champlain_Provincial_Park "Samuel de Champlain Provincial Park"), a popular summer camping spot, was particularly affected by an EF2-rated downburst; hundreds were left stranded due to flash flooding and a particularly strong downburst which downed trees and power lines, blocking off roads, and injured several people.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CPnug-7)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-CPbay-62)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-63) Similar severe weather effects were felt in other areas, such as [Algonquin Provincial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algonquin_Provincial_Park "Algonquin Provincial Park"), where two separate downbursts occurred in the area. One of the two caused a tree to fall on a tent, injuring a boy camping with his mother.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-64)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-65)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-66) Finally, in [Mallorytown, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_of_Yonge "Front of Yonge"), another downburst uprooted several trees, one of which fell on a tent occupied by a father with his young child; the father was killed while the child survived with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-cbcMT-67) Several municipalities declared states of emergency due to the "devastation" brought by the severe storms.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-68) Several downbursts were reported in [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec") on the nighth of June 23.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6) Overall, the downbursts in Canada caused one fatality and at least four injuries.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_and_derecho_of_June_19%E2%80%9322,_2025#cite_note-NTP-6) This same line of storms also pushed into [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_/(state/) "New York (state)") on June 22, causing severe wind gusts, some up to 70 mph (110 km/h), which downed trees and power lines. 2025

The 2025 tornado season is the ongoing season of tornadoes and tornado outbreaks worldwide in the year 2025. Strong and destructive tornadoes form most frequently in the United States, China, the Pampas, the European Plain, South Africa, and Bengal, but they can occur almost anywhere under the right conditions. Tornadoes also develop occasionally in southern Canada during the Northern Hemisphere's summer and somewhat regularly at other times of the year across Europe, Asia, and Australia. Tornadic events are often accompanied by other forms of severe weather, including strong thunderstorms, winds, and hail.
Worldwide, at least 100 tornado-related deaths have been confirmed – 67 in the United States, 12 in Vietnam, seven in Brazil, four each in China and Spain, two in the Philippines, and one each in France, Japan, Portugal, and Turkey.
2025 featured the first EF5 tornado since the 2013 Moore tornado, which occurred near Enderlin, North Dakota on June 20. It also featured the most violent tornadoes in a year since 2013, with eight tornadoes worldwide receiving a rating of (E)F4 or higher. Six of these tornadoes occurred in the United States, and two in Brazil. 2025 also had the least active late season since 2012, with only 149 tornadoes occurring from August to December, compared to 1,106 tornadoes from March to June.

January[edit]
January 1 (Argentina)[edit]
On the afternoon of January 1, a multiple-vortex tornado briefly touched down in Mar Chiquita, Buenos Aires. It was caused by the same storm system that had caused a tornado in Oncativo, Córdoba, the night before, on December 31, 2024.[2][3]

The Tehama County, California EFU tornado on January 3, 2025.
From January 3 to January 7, a major winter storm passed over the contiguous United States. The storm system made landfall on January 3 over the West Coast of the United States,[4][better source needed] where it produced the first tornado of the year, a brief EFU tornado in rural Tehama County, California, which caused no damage.[5][6] On January 4, a low pressure system organized over the Texas Panhandle and Oklahoma. Interacting with the pre-established cold temperatures, the system's warm front was predicted to generate severe thunderstorms across Southern United States the following day, prompting the Storm Prediction Center to issue an enhanced risk for the region. The outlook included a 10% risk area for tornadoes, along with the potential for large hail and damaging winds.[7][8]

High-end EF2 damage to a well-constructed shop building east of Marion, Louisiana.
On January 5, a small tornado outbreak occurred as a squall line of severe thunderstorms passed through the region, producing multiple tornadoes in Louisiana, Arkansas, Mississippi, and Alabama, a couple of which were strong. A high-end EF2 tornado touched down near Marion, Louisiana, completely destroying a mobile home and a well-built shop building, damaging the roofs of multiple houses, and snapping many large trees. In Mississippi, a low-end EF2 tornado snapped or uprooted numerous trees and downed power poles as it passed to the north of Brooksville. High-end EF1 tornadoes caused moderate tree and structure damage in the rural Mississippi communities of Boon and Gwinville as well. An EF1 tornado near Pelahatchie prompted a PDS tornado warning,[9] damaged chicken houses, downed trees and power lines, and caused an indirect injury when a train ran into a downed tree that had fallen onto railroad tracks.[10] A total of 14 tornadoes were confirmed, resulting in one indirect injury and no fatalities.[11]

January 6 (Saudi Arabia)[edit]
As a red alert for severe weather was issued by the National Centre of Meteorology over the region around Mecca on January 6, a tornado was reported to have struck Rabigh, which was reported by Gulf News to be the strongest ever recorded in the coastal region of Saudi Arabia. The National Centre of Meteorology also discussed plans to further research the tornado.[12]

Storm Gabri struck Italy on January 17, causing torrential rainfall, thunderstorms, strong winds, and multiple tornadoes, especially on the island of Sicily. An IF2 tornado impacted areas near Catania, causing significant roof and tree damage, bending a metal truss electrical transmission tower in half, and rolling a roulotte trailer 30 m (33 yd). Metal light poles were also bent, a semi-trailer was overturned, and sheet metal from buildings was scattered 500 m (550 yd) up a hillside. A long-tracked multiple-vortex IF2 tornado that struck areas outside of Avola downed numerous trees and power lines, toppled another electrical transmission tower, destroyed a masonry outbuilding, unroofed a house, and damaged the roofs of other homes.[13] In Augusta, an IF0.5 tornado overturned a small ape car, damaged concrete monuments and decorations at a cemetery, downed trees and power lines, and tore sheet metal roofing from buildings. An IF1 tornado struck the outskirts of Licata as well, damaging crops and destroying greenhouses. A total of five tornadoes were confirmed.[13][14][15]

January 21 (Portugal)[edit]
Storm Garoé made landfall in Spain and Portugal on January 21, bringing strong winds, torrential rain, and severe weather in coastal areas.[16] During the late evening, an IF2 tornado tracked through rural areas near the community of Montevil in Setúbal District, Portugal. Many large trees were snapped or uprooted along the path, and some were defoliated and stripped of their branches. Some crop damage also occurred, and power lines were downed.[13]

January 23 (United Kingdom)[edit]
Main article: Storm Éowyn
On January 23, Storm Éowyn made landfall in United Kingdom, resulting in strong winds and heavy rain. An IF2 tornado moved through Holywell and Quintrell Downs, causing severe damage at the Trevornick Caravan Park, snapping many trees, and causing roof damage to homes. Multiple mobile homes and RVs were tossed and destroyed at the caravan park, resulting in one injury.[13][17]

January 26 (New Zealand)[edit]
A low-pressure system organized to the west of New Zealand, causing heavy rain and severe thunderstorms on the North Island.[18] In the early morning of January 26, a damaging tornado hit Mangawhai and surrounding areas in the Northland Region, downing many trees, snapping concrete power poles, and ripping roofs off of homes. A media business sustained extensive structural damage, cars were damaged, debris was left deposited in trees, and two people were seriously injured. There was damage to about 50 properties, and about 4,700 homes lost power.[19][20] The tornado was not officially rated, but was estimated to have reached high-end EF1 or low-end EF2 intensity.[21]

On January 27, a damaging IF2 tornado struck Torre de Juan Abad, Spain. The strong tornado tracked through the northern part of town, causing significant damage to cars, homes, restaurants, auto repair shops, and warehouses. Several brick and masonry buildings suffered major structural damage, including total roof loss and collapse of multiple exterior walls. The tornado also severely damaged farms in agricultural areas, and snapped or uprooted more than 1,000 olive trees. In England, a tornado downed trees and destroyed some sheds near Whitchurch Hill, and was rated IF1.[13]

A mobile home that was destroyed at high-end EF2 intensity near Deer Lodge, Tennessee, resulting in two fatalities.
On February 5, a winter storm hit the Ohio Valley, bringing the possibility of severe weather and a few tornadoes on the warm side of the system in Kentucky and Tennessee. A line of severe thunderstorms impacted the region later that night and continued into the early morning hours of February 6. The storms produced several tornadoes, a couple of which were strong. Three tornadoes occurred in Kentucky, including an EF1 tornado near Island City in Owsley County. The tornado snapped or uprooted trees, destroyed a small shed-like residence,  damaged two mobile homes, and was only the third tornado to be confirmed in the county since reliable records began in 1950. Two other EF1 tornadoes passed near Magnolia and Dango, downing trees, inflicting minor to moderate damage to homes, and damaging or destroying multiple barns and outbuildings.[11] In Tennessee, a high-end EF2 tornado snapped or uprooted countless trees in wooded areas and completely destroyed two mobile homes near the community of Deer Lodge, killing two people in one of them and injuring two others. Another EF2 tornado touched down near Center Grove, causing major tree damage and destroying multiple barns. Two EF1 tornadoes that touched down near Algood and Crawford downed many trees, inflicted minor to moderate damage to various structures, and injured one person each. The final tornado of the event caused high-end EF1 damage near Thorn Hill, destroying a barn, overturning a tanker trailer, and inflicting window and siding damage to a church. A total of eight tornadoes were confirmed, resulting in two fatalities and four injuries.[22][23][24][11]

February 11 (Spain)[edit]
An IF2 tornado the community of Pozo del Camino in Andalusia, Spain. More than 30 homes were damaged, trees and power lines were downed, and a free-standing masonry wall was blown over.[25][13]

Major tree damage and an obliterated mobile home following an EF3 tornado near Whistler, Mississippi.
A second, more potent storm system impacted the southeast on February 12, bringing severe thunderstorms and a risk of tornadoes.[26][27] That evening, a few tornadoes touched down in Mississippi and Alabama, including two strong tornadoes. In Mississippi, a high-end EF0 tornado moved through the east side of Columbia, heavily damaging a hardware store, destroying a few sheds, and damaging the roofs of homes in town. A supercell in Wayne County produced a powerful multiple-vortex EF3 tornado that touched down in a rural area to the east of Laurel before it tracked to the northeast near Whistler and dissipated near Matherville, prompting a PDS tornado warning.[28][29][better source needed] The tornado inflicted major structural damage to a few frame homes, and several mobile homes were completely swept away and obliterated, with their metal frames and debris strewn hundreds of yards across fields. Wooded areas suffered total deforestation, including large trees that were snapped, stripped of their branches, and sustained partial debarking. Some ground scouring also occurred, while a pickup truck, pieces of farming equipment, and RVs were thrown and destroyed as well.[28] In Alabama, A low-end EF2 tornado passed near Tattlersville, prompting another PDS tornado warning to be issued.[30][28] The tornado snapped or uprooted many trees in remote wooded areas and destroyed a poorly constructed house. A total of five tornadoes were confirmed, resulting in no fatalities and three injuries.[11] The severe weather was also associated with a winter storm, which resulted in a fatality in Missouri.[31]

A winter storm brought heavy rain and strong winds to Southern California on February 13, producing a high-end EF0 tornado that damaged mobile homes in Oxnard.[32][33] Moving across the United States, the storm system produced severe thunderstorms and tornadoes throughout the Deep South from February 15–16.[34] Tornadoes were confirmed in Kentucky, Tennessee,[35] Mississippi,[35][36] Alabama,[37][38][39] Louisiana,[40] and Georgia,[41] including a couple of strong tornadoes. The tornadoes were embedded in a fast-moving squall line, including an EF2 tornado that heavily damaged homes, destroyed a barn, and downed large trees near Bradford, Tennessee. In Alabama, another EF2 tornado touched down outside of Russellville and impacted areas in and around the small community of Waco, tearing the roof off of a house, destroying a silo and several outbuildings, tossing an ATV, and downing many trees and power lines. An EF1 tornado moved through Tuscumbia and Muscle Shoals, unroofing a school and another building. The towns of Collinsville, Mississippi and Rogersville, Alabama were also hit by EF1 tornadoes, resulting in minor to moderate damage.[39][11] A total of 25 tornadoes were confirmed, resulting in no fatalities and two injuries. The storm system also spawned heavy winds in the Northeastern United States, with hurricane-force winds recorded at Camp David. One woman died due to the high winds in Philadelphia when a tree fell on her vehicle.[42]

Main article: Early March 2025 North American blizzard
In early March, a storm system with intense wind shear brought strong winds and warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico to the southern Great Plains and the Deep South, creating a severe weather setup with the chance for severe thunderstorms and a few strong tornadoes. On March 4, the Storm Prediction Center issued an enhanced risk, including a 10% significant tornado risk.[43][44] Numerous weak tornadoes touched down later that afternoon and evening across Oklahoma, Texas, and Louisiana, including an EF1 tornado that struck Ada, Oklahoma, destroying an old brick building, causing considerable damage to several apartment buildings, businesses, and a school, and injuring one person.[45][46][47] In Texas, a high-end EF1 tornado impacted Irving, where apartment buildings and the Irving Police Academy Family Advocacy building had partial roof loss. Another high-end EF1 tornado snapped many trees, destroyed a large metal outbuilding, and overturned campers on the property of the Barry Telford Unit prison, and caused minor tree damage in the southern part of New Boston before dissipating.[11] In Louisiana, an EF1 tornado caused minor damage on the north side of Shreveport, and another EF1 tornado damaged homes and downed trees in Boyce.[11] Later that night, the storms moved into Mississippi and produced a strong EF2 tornado that touched down near Whistler in Wayne County, near the same area that was hit by an EF3 tornado the previous month on February 12. The tornado completely destroyed a few mobile homes and chicken houses, heavily damaged a couple of frame homes, tossed vehicles, and injured four people. Two additional weak tornadoes occurred in North Carolina and Virginia on March 5 before the outbreak came to an end. A total of 39 tornadoes were confirmed, resulting in no fatalities and 11 injuries.[11]

Main articles: Tornado outbreak of March 13–16, 2025; List of tornadoes in the outbreak of March 13–16, 2025; and 2025 Kentwood–Carson tornado
Doorbell camera still of a violent EF4 tornado that struck Diaz, Arkansas in the nighttime hours of March 14.
A destructive and deadly tornado outbreak occurred across mainly portions of the Midwestern and Southeastern United States between March 13–16. On March 13, a trough moved through the West Coast,[48] spawning a high-end EF0 tornado in the Los Angeles area.[49] The Storm Prediction Center issued a moderate risk for severe weather for parts of the Midwest and Southeast on March 14 as the trough moved west over the Rockies.[50] The Day 2 outlook was upgraded to a tornado-driven high risk area for portions of Mississippi and Alabama, making it the third ever issuance of a Day 2 high risk, with the previous two being for April 7, 2006 and April 14, 2012.[51]
On March 14, a moderate risk for severe weather was issued for the much of Iowa, Illinois, and Missouri, with a 15% risk for significant tornadoes centered around Southern Illinois and Southeastern Missouri.[50] In the early evening, a PDS tornado watch was issued for portions of Southeast Missouri, Northeast Arkansas, Northern Mississippi, and more.[52] Among the tornadoes that touched down that day were a long-track, high-end EF3 tornado that tracked through southern Missouri and prompted the issuance of a tornado emergency for Fremont and Van Buren,[53][54] an EF2 tornado that moved into the Greater St. Louis area, notably crossing a St. Louis Lambert International Airport runway while a plane was taking off,[55][56] a high-end EF4 tornado that caused catastrophic damage to rural neighborhood northwest of Diaz, Arkansas,[57] a very long-track, low-end EF4 tornado that struck near Fifty-Six and Franklin, Arkansas,[57] an EF3 tornado that killed three people in Bakersfield, Missouri,[58] a long-track, high-end EF3 tornado that went through Cushman and Cave City, Arkansas, killing three,[57] and a low-end EF3 tornado that killed one person after ripping through a trailer park near Poplar Bluff, Missouri,[53][59][60] Overall, 10 people in Missouri and three more in Arkansas were killed by tornadoes on the 14th.[61][62]

A well-anchored two-story home swept away at low-end EF4 intensity near Tylertown, Mississippi.
On March 15, the high risk area continued into the Day 1 Outlook, including a 30 percent risk for significant tornadoes in central Mississippi and Alabama.[63] In the late morning, a PDS tornado watch was issued for parts of Louisiana and nearly all of Mississippi[64] and later much of Alabama[65] as a tornado outbreak featuring "significant tornadoes, some of which should be long-track and potentially violent," was expected throughout the afternoon and evening.[63] In the early afternoon, a tornado emergency was issued for parts of Walthall, Lawrence, Marion, and Jefferson Davis counties in Mississippi[66][67] as a large, violent, long-track EF4 tornado was moving through the area; at least five people were killed and at least three others were injured by this tornado.[68] An EF2 tornado intersected its path just 41 minutes later. Another deadly EF3 tornado also tracked just east of the path of the long-track EF4 tornado, touching down while the latter was still on the ground.[68] Tornadoes continued in Mississippi and Alabama throughout the afternoon and evening, including an EF2 tornado that struck Winterboro, Alabama, damaging a high school and killing one person, and an EF3 that killed two people near Plantersville, Alabama.[69] Overall, seven people were killed in Mississippi and three more were killed in Alabama from tornadoes on the 15th.[70][71]
On March 16, a slight risk for tornadoes was issued for the South Atlantic States[72] as several weak tornadoes touched down across the East Coast. In all, 118 tornadoes were confirmed in the outbreak, making this the largest tornado outbreak ever recorded in March. In addition, 42 people were killed from this outbreak,[73] including 23 tornadic deaths: Ten in Missouri, seven in Mississippi, and three each in Arkansas and Alabama.

Radar animation of the tornado outbreak and floods.
A slow-moving weather system resulted in both a devastating tornado outbreak as well as historic life-threatening flash floods throughout the Southern and Midwestern United States from April 2–7, spawning 157 tornadoes in total. The Storm Prediction Center (SPC) issued a high risk for the first day of the outbreak, April 2, which was be the busiest day as 74 tornadoes touched down across nine states. That evening, a high-end EF3 tornado destroyed multiple homes near Latty, Missouri. Later, a large, multiple-vortex high-end EF3 tornado impacted Bay, Lake City, and Monette, Arkansas, derailing two freight trains, and destroying high-tension power line trusses and several homes. A tornado emergency was declared for Lake City as the tornado struck,[83][84] and injured eight people.[85] Additionally, one indirect fatality occurred in association with an EF2 tornado that passed through Delta, Missouri as it moved along Route 25; this tornado damaged approximately 200 structures along its path.[86][87] Tornado continued throughout the overnight hours into April 3. Another EF3 tornado damaged or destroyed buildings on the east side of Jeffersontown, Kentucky while an EF2 tornado injured three people along the Mississippi-Tennessee state line northwest of Walnut, Mississippi.[11] A destructive high-end EF3 tornado devastated Selmer, Tennessee, heavily damaging or destroying homes and businesses, obliterating manufactured homes, and killing five people.[85] Soon after, a second tornado emergency was issued as another large, long-track high-end EF3 tornado passed near Slayden, Mississippi before crossing the state line and striking Grand Junction, Tennessee at EF2 strength, heavily damaging or destroying several homes, businesses, and manufactured homes, and collapsing a metal truss tower along its path. Two people were killed and three others were injured in a mobile home that was obliterated as the tornado crossed the state line.[85][88]
Relatively lower, but still significant, tornadic activity continued over the next several days. On April 4, an EF2 tornado impacted the Lone Star, Texas area, heavily damaging homes, snapping trees, and tossing six vehicles.[89] The next morning on April 5, another EF2 tornado damaged or destroyed outbuilding and manufactured homes and injured one person near Wynne, Arkansas.[90] Later, a long-tracked EF2 tornado caused widespread damage to homes, outbuildings, power poles, and trees as it passed near Thaxton, Hurricane, and New Albany, Mississippi.[90] On April 6, an EF2 tornado struck Stringer, Mississippi killing a person in a mobile home that was obliterated.[68] Weak tornadoes were observed on April 7 as the outbreak came to an end.[11] Overall, nine tornadic fatalities occurred as a result of this outbreak, with many more being killed by the devastating flooding that accompanied it.[91]

A four-day outbreak of tornadoes took place from April 17–20 across the Midwest and parts of the South as a slow-moving upper-level trough moved through the region. On April 17, an intense tornado touched down northeast of Bennington, Nebraska, producing low-end EF3 damage before later causing additional damage in Nashville.[93] Additionally, a very large high-end EF1 tornado prompted the issuance of a tornado emergency for the city of Essex, Iowa.[94] Tornado activity remained relatively low for the remainder of the outbreak, though a high-end EF1 tornado killed one and injured two as it destroyed homes in the town of Spaulding, Oklahoma on April 20. This was the only tornadic fatality of the outbreak.[95] However, two people were killed due to flooding related to the storm system in Oklahoma.[96]

A tornado outbreak lasting 4 days took place across parts of the Midwest, Southern United States, and Great Plains regions of the US from April 27–30. On April 27, activity was focused on Nebraska, with several tornadoes, including three rated EF2, being confirmed. The Bingham-Ashby tornado in particular was the widest ever confirmed by the National Weather Service in North Platte, at 2,200 yards (2,000 m).[97] The following day, a moderate risk of severe weather was forecast, driven by a 15% chance for significant tornadoes; this moderate risk was centered on the Upper Midwest region of the United States.[98] Activity largely failed to materialize, with just 12 tornadoes being confirmed, seven of which occurred in Wisconsin.[99] More severe weather occurred the following day, with tornadoes occurring in Oklahoma, Arkansas, Missouri and Texas. The strongest of these tornadoes was rated EF3 after tearing through parts of Seymour, Texas, including the Seymour Airport.[100] The outbreak concluded the next day, with several more tornadoes being confirmed, including one rated EF2 after damaging multiple farms in Fayette County, Illinois.[101] In all, 48 tornadoes were confirmed in this outbreak.

A severe weather outbreak produced scattered tornadoes across Europe from May 2–4, producing a total of 11 tornadoes across several countries. On May 2, conditions in Iberia, namely a cold front pulling warm, moist air from the Mediterranean into an unstable environment with high wind shear, allowed for the development of long-lasting supercells.[102] Two tornadoes touched down in southeastern Portugal: one IF1.5 tornado near Beja caused significant roof damage[103][13] while another IF2 tornado near Campo Maior caused widespread damage to the neighborhood of Degolados and injured one person.[103][104] Remnants of this system continued to create a risk of severe weather in Portugal the next day,[105] as a waterspout moved ashore off the coast of Sesimbra and a large IF1.5 tornado tracked through Sardoal in central Portugal.[103] Similar conditions in parts of Southern Europe[102] spawned an IF1.5 tornado in Turkey on May 3 and a landspout tornado in Cyprus the next day.[13] Throughout Central Europe, conditions were similar to Iberia, supporting supercell development.[105] Three tornadoes ravaged forests and damaged buildings throughout Germany on May 3,[13] and the weakening system produced a final weak tornado in Belarus the next day, concluding the outbreak.[13]

May 4 (Guadeloupe)[edit]
A very rare tornado struck the town of Baie-Mahault in central Guadeloupe, causing minor structural damage. Metal roof sheets were lifted into the air, trees were snapped or uprooted, and electrical wires were snapped.[106][107]

May 8 (China)[edit]
A strong tornado struck Qidong County in Hengyang, Hunan Province. Two people were killed when their house collapsed, and several more were injured.[108][109][110] Six houses collapsed and more than 100 were damaged.[111]

On May 8, two tornadoes touched down in Rio Grande do Sul.[112] The next day, a wide tornado struck Erval Grande, being officially rated an EF2 by the PREVOTS group.[113][114] The event lasted about 15 minutes, damaging around 285 homes, displacing 55 families, and overall affecting over 1,000 people. The storm also wrecked power lines and blocked roads with fallen trees. The mayor declared a state of emergency, and relief efforts provided shelter and supplies.[115][116][117] Additionally, a tornado struck Palmitos in Santa Catarina, killing one man when a tree hit him.[118] Another damaging tornado was confirmed in Santo Amaro da Imperatriz.[118][119]

Main articles: Tornado outbreak of May 15–16, 2025; List of tornadoes in the outbreak of May 15–16, 2025; 2025 St. Louis tornado; and 2025 Somerset–London tornado
A two story home south of Marion, Illinois swept away at high-end EF4 intensity.
A significant tornado outbreak produced 60 tornadoes in portions of the Midwestern and Southeastern United States on May 15–16 due to a negatively tilted mid-level atmospheric trough that moved through the Upper Midwest. On May 15, tornadic activity was centered on the Great Lakes Region with 31 tornadoes touching down throughout the day.[120] An EF2 tornado damaged several structures near Colby, Wisconsin.[121] One supercell thunderstorm produced six tornadoes, including an EF2 tornado that injured one person as it passed through Juneau, and another EF2 tornado that struck Mayville. Four more tornadoes touched down from this initial round of storms after midnight as well.[11]
A moderate risk of severe weather was issued for parts of the Mid-South and Midwest for May 16 due to the possibility of several long-tracked, intense tornadoes that afternoon and evening.[122] An early afternoon EF3 tornado struck the Greater St. Louis area, causing widespread destruction to trees, power lines, homes, traffic lights, and other structures, killing four people, and injuring 38 others.[11][123] Another deadly EF3 tornado destroyed homes and mobile homes and killed two more people near Blodgett, Missouri.[11][124][125][126][127] A stray high-end EF1 tornado also caused considerable damage in Baltimore, Maryland.[128] A violent high-end EF4 tornado injured seven people and prompted the issuance of a tornado emergency to be issued for the Marion, Illinois area.[129] A strong EF2 tornado in Linton killed one person. In Kentucky, an EF3 tornado caused intense damage in the Morganfield area, and a destructive EF4 tornado struck the cities of Somerset and London, killing 19 people. Overall, 26 tornadic fatalities occurred as a result of this tornado outbreak.[11][130]

Main articles: Tornado outbreak of May 18–21, 2025 and List of tornadoes in the outbreak of May 18–21, 2025
Mobile home swept away at low-end EF2 intensity in Grinnell, Kansas.
Another powerful trough ejection, coupled with deep moisture return from the  Gulf of Mexico, prompted another damaging tornado outbreak, moving from the Southern Great Plains towards the Southeast. Numerous tornadoes touched down, several of which were strong to intense. On the May 18, an EF3 tornado caused severe damage in the town of Grinnell, Kansas across its long path,[11] while an EF1 tornado caused four injuries when it struck Gordon, Texas.[131] After dark, a powerful, cyclic supercell developed in south-central Kansas, eventually producing a long family of eight tornadoes, five of which were rated EF3. Two of these prompted tornado emergencies: one as it approached the towns of Greensburg and Brenham,[132] and another that directly hit the small town of Plevna.[133][11] Tornado activity shifted towards the Southeast by May 20,[134] and in the evening, another tornado emergency was issued for an EF2 tornado that went through Madison, Alabama, dissipating just before reaching Huntsville.[135][11] In all, 133 tornadoes were confirmed from the outbreak.

May 25 (Chile)[edit]
President of Chile Gabriel Boric surveys EF1 tornado damage in Puerto Varas.
A tornado struck the city of Puerto Varas, Chile, in the Los Lagos Region, injuring 13 people and damaging 250 homes. It was preliminarily rated EF1 by the Chilean Meteorological Directorate.[136][137]
The storm impacted 150–250 homes, a supermarket, and infrastructure, including power lines, resulting in over 10,000 households losing electricity.[138]

A small tornado event, which produced 18 tornadoes over 2 days, took place mainly across the Southeastern United States on May 29–30. On May 29, a strong EF2 tornado struck Locust Grove, Georgia. Two people were thrown from their house as the tornado demolished their home, injuring both, one critically. The tornado was then caught on video crossing I-75.[139][140] In addition, 3 rare tornadoes touched down in the Western United States. 2 in Utah, specifically in Herriman[141] and Logan[142]. The other happened in Loving, New Mexico[143]. Early the following morning, a strong EF2 tornado struck in rural Washington County, Kentucky. Several homes, mobile homes, and outbuildings were heavily damaged or destroyed by the tornado, which killed one person and injured 14 others.[144] In addition, an unwarned EF0 tornado rolled campers, damaged homes and barns, and injured five people southwest of Loudon, Tennessee.[145]

June 1 (France)[edit]
A strong tornado affected the Loire area, particularly the communes of Lérigneux and Roche-en-Forez. Several houses had their roofs partially or completely ripped off, and significant tree damage was also observed. Additionally, one person was injured. The tornado was officially rated an IF2.[13]

June 3 (Australia)[edit]
A tornado near the town of Frankland River, Western Australia destroyed trees, damaged vehicles, and injured a farmhand.[146]

A single supercell produced a family of eight tornadoes as it moved eastward towards the Lubbock, Texas metropolitan area.[147] The second tornado was a large, strong EF2 tornado that moved through open desert near the town of Morton, flipping center pivots and snapping wooden power poles.[11] The tornado was highly photographed and videoed by nearby storm chasers, and it was researched by nearby research teams during the LIFT Project. Dr. Sean Waugh, with the National Severe Storms Laboratory (NSSL), researched the tornado. Using the NSSL Hail Camera Truck, positioned 200 metres (220 yd) away from the tornado, he captured a 1.6-inch-diameter (4.1 cm) hailstone that was "being ejected from the tornado" at speeds up to 202 mph (325 km/h). The hailstone was only visible to the camera for six frames; a total of 0.0182 seconds.[148] The supercell also produced two other EF2 tornadoes along with two EF1 tornadoes and three EFU tornadoes. One of the EF1 tornadoes injured two people in a trailer park northeast of Smyer. A swath of very strong outflow winds up to 115 mph (185 km/h) and very large hail up to 2.5 in (6.4 cm) in diameter impacted western and southwestern Lubbock following the dissipation of the final tornado. Windows and skylights were shattered, and trees and roofs were damaged throughout this area.[147] Two other weak tornadoes also touched down earlier that day.[11]

June 15 (Armenia)[edit]
An IF1.5 tornado injured five people as it moved through Aparan and Lusagyugh, Armenia, causing widespread, considerable damage. Several homes, apartment buildings, schools, and other structures were affected.[13]

At least 14 tornadoes touched down in unpopulated areas of Russia. On June 17, a long track F3/IF1.5 tornado tracked through Khanty-Mansia.[149][13] It was found to be over 2.5 km (1.6 mi) wide, tying it for the widest tornado ever recorded in Russia. The tornado was likely stronger than its rating, but the only damage it inflicted was to trees.[13] The next day, an IF2 tornado snapped reinforced concrete power poles.[13]

A period of enhanced severe weather occurred across both the northern part of the US (in particular North Dakota), and the southern part of Canada (in particular Saskatchewan) from June 19–22. Environment Canada confirmed that 10 tornadoes touched down in Saskatchewan, two of which produced EF2 damage on June 19.[150] During June 20, a large and intense tornado impacted a farmstead near Spiritwood, destroyed a large steel building and severely damaged a two-story home at mid-range EF3 intensity. One EF2 tornado was confirmed in the Valley City area as well. One very large and exceptionally violent tornado occurred near Enderlin, tossing train cars, destroying farmsteads, and killing three people.[151][152][11] The tornado was reclassified from an EF3 to an EF5 on October 6, 2025, after a reanalysis confirmed wind speeds exceeded the EF5 threshold. The upgrade was prompted by the tornado derailing 33 train cars,[153] an event that was not initially used for damage assessment but became a key factor based on new research. This reclassification marks the first EF5 tornado in the U.S. in 12 years, since the 2013 Moore, Oklahoma tornado.[154] A powerful derecho also produced hurricane-force winds across Montana, North Dakota, Minnesota, and South Dakota, with the highest confirmed wind gust reaching 120 mph (190 km/h).[155] The remnants of the system, a line of thunderstorms, moved into New York by the early morning hours of June 22, spawning an EF1 tornado that struck Clark Mills. The tornado snapped and uprooted many trees, with several trees falling on homes, which resulted in three fatalities.[156]

A small tornado event occurred late on June 28 and into the early morning of June 29 across South Dakota and Southern Minnesota. At least five tornadoes were confirmed, along with several more under investigation, awaiting confirmation and rating. The first tornado of the night, rated EF2, touched down near Altamont, South Dakota. This storm would cycle, first producing a brief EFU-rated tornado, then the supercell cycled again and produced a high-end EF3 tornado near east of Clear Lake, South Dakota. This tornado exhibited multiple vortex breakdowns, crossed SD 22 in a narrow “drill bit” formation, and impacted a farmstead at high-end EF3 intensity. A two-story farm home was completely swept away, several vehicles were thrown and were majorly mangled, trees were debarked, and several outbuildings and silos were destroyed. Two people were injured before the tornado dissipated southwest of Gary.[157] During the early morning hours of June 29, several QLCS tornadoes were reported in the suburbs of Minneapolis, Minnesota.[11]

July[edit]
July 2 (China)[edit]
A strong tornado struck industrial areas of Cangzhou, China. Multiple factories and other buildings were levelled and vehicles were thrown long distances. Two fatalities and multiple injuries were reported. No official rating has been released.[158][159]

July 12 (Utah)[edit]
In a rare occurrence, a nearly stationary and strong fire tornado was produced by the Deer Creek Fire in San Juan County, Utah, with winds rated at 122 mph (196 km/h) by the NWS, giving it a rating of EF2. No injuries or fatalities occurred due to this tornado, although a fire engine belonging to the Bureau of Land Management was damaged.[160][161] This is the second tornado that has been rated EF2 in Utah.[162]

July 23 (Australia)[edit]
A tornado in Perth, Australia damaged 'multi-million-dollar' homes and 'uprooted trees'. This tornado likely started as a waterspout before causing damage in the Perth suburb of City Beach.[163]

Back-to-back days of tornado activity focused over South Dakota. On July 27, a strong, photogenic tornado occurred west of Watertown. The tornado inflicted significant damage to a farmstead where a garage was swept from its foundation, and the main residence had only interior walls left standing. Significant tree damage was also observed.[11][164] The next day on July 28, an isolated supercell produced three separate tornadoes in Gregory County. The strongest of them was an EF2 tornado that broke wooden power poles and inflicted major damage to a single-family residence and two nearby outbuildings. The tornado lifted just before entering the city of Bonesteel.[165]

August[edit]
August 3 (Russia)[edit]
A significant tornado affected the Jewish Autonomous Oblast of Russia, bending several power transmission towers. The tornado was rated IF2.[13]
August 25–26 (Typhoon Kajiki)[edit]
Two days of tornadic unrest began late in the evening on August 25, as Typhoon Kajiki made landfall in Vietnam. A powerful tornado struck Kim Bảng district in Ninh Bình.[166] The tornado, though lasting only a few minutes, caused extensive damage to more than 200 homes and businesses. One 88-year-old woman was killed after a wall collapsed onto her, and 14 others were hospitalized with injuries. The following day, four additional tornadoes were reported across northern Vietnam. In total, the two-day outbreak resulted in at least one fatality and 14 reported injuries.[167][168]
